spans.v: Kotlin is a modern, statically typed programming language developed by JetBrains. It runs on the JVM (Java Virtual Machine), and it can also compile to JavaScript, native machine code and WebAssembly.

The reason Kotlin was created is simple: JetBrains wrote its own products (IntelliJ IDEA and others) in Java, and they were tired of Java's verbosity, null errors and dated type system. The existing alternatives (Scala, Groovy) were either too complex or compiled too slowly. So they built their own language —
The type system separates types that can hold null from types that can't. The "billion-dollar mistake" is caught at compile time, not on the user's phone.
The same functionality takes on average 30–40% fewer lines than in Java.
generates 5 methods in a single line.
Java and Kotlin files can live side by side in the same project. All existing Java libraries just work — nothing has to be rewritten.
Write asynchronous code as if it were synchronous. Thousands of concurrent operations are handled without creating threads.
One business logic — Android, iOS, desktop, backend and web. Only the UI part is written per platform.
Google has declared Android "Kotlin-first". Netflix, Uber, Pinterest, Trello and Duolingo use it in production.

spans.v: Kotlin didn't appear overnight. Each of its versions solved a concrete, practical problem. The timeline below shows how the language took shape.

desc.v: JetBrains' Saint Petersburg team starts working on a new language for internal needs. The goal: compilation as fast as Java's and a type system as powerful as Scala's.
The language is officially unveiled. The name comes from
near Saint Petersburg — following the tradition of Java being named after the island of Java.
The source code is published on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license. Community contributions begin.
The first production-ready version. It comes with a backward-compatibility guarantee: code written today will work in future 1.x versions.

items.title: Google announces official support for Android

desc.v: At the Google I/O conference, Kotlin is announced as a first-class language for Android. It was the moment that changed the language's fate.
The coroutine API for asynchronous programming leaves experimental status. The end of callback hell.
Google states that from now on new Android APIs will be designed for Kotlin first (the Jetpack KTX libraries).
The fully Kotlin-based declarative UI framework becomes stable. XML layouts gradually fade into the background.
KMP is declared production-ready. Sharing business logic between Android and iOS becomes a real option.
A completely rewritten frontend. Compilation gets up to 2x faster, smart casts get smarter and IDE response times drop.
Work continues on Kotlin/Wasm, context parameters, richer error handling and iOS support in Compose Multiplatform.

fun main() {
    val i: Int = 42

    // val l: Long = i        ← ERROR: Type mismatch
    val l: Long = i.toLong()  // correct
    val d: Double = i.toDouble()
    val s: String = i.toString()

    println(i)
    println(l)
    println(d)
    println(s)

    // Between Char and Int
    val c: Char = 'K'
    println(c)
    println(c.code)           // 75 — the Unicode code

    // From text to number — the safe way
    val bosla: Int? = "abc".toIntOrNull()   // null, doesn't throw
    val yaxsi: Int = "123".toInt()          // 123
}

blocks.text: Do I need to know Java before learning Kotlin?

spans.v: No. Learning Kotlin as your first language is entirely possible, and in many cases it's even easier — less boilerplate, clearer error messages. Knowing Java only helps when you're reading older libraries.
On Android, it practically already has. On the backend, though, Java is still dominant and will stay that way for a long time. The two aren't rivals — they live together on the same platform.
No. It compiles to the same bytecode, and its performance is practically the same as Java's. Compilation used to be slow, but the K2 compiler solved that problem.
